stops.name: La Real, the abbey of the grey monks, the Art set down
stops.campa: Coming down from Randa, Ramon does not go home but to the nearby Cistercian abbey of La Real, outside Palma, and asks the monks for a cell and ink. There, before the illumination can fade, he sets down the first version of what he calls the Ars compendiosa inveniendi veritatem, the Brief Art of Finding Truth, built on the great circling Figure A, whose letters spell out the Dignities of God, Goodness, Greatness, Eternity, Power, Wisdom, and the rest, turning against one another on concentric wheels to generate, mechanically and without appeal to authority, every proof the missionary's tongue will need.

stops.name: Montpellier, summoned by the young King of Majorca
stops.campa: James II, newly enthroned as king of an independent Majorca and already Ramon's acquaintance from the seneschal years, summons him to his court in exile at Montpellier, the mainland city that is half capital to the island kingdom. Here Ramon lays before the king the whole of his design: the Art now written, and beyond it a plan for a house where friars might learn Arabic before ever setting foot among the Saracens, so the sermon might follow directly on the grammar lesson. James, moved by the argument or by old loyalty to his former servant, takes the plan to heart and to Rome.

stops.name: Miramar, the monastery of tongues confirmed by Rome
stops.campa: On the cliff road between Valldemossa and Deià, above the sea, King James founds the monastery he and Ramon have planned: Miramar, house of thirteen Franciscan brothers set apart to do nothing but learn Arabic, so missionaries might go out at last equipped with the very tongue of those they mean to turn. On the seventeenth of October Pope John XXI signs the bull confirming the foundation and its royal endowment. It is the first working piece of Ramon's three resolves made real in stone and rule, a decade after the visions in his chamber, and it will outlast the century.

stops.name: Montpellier, Blanquerna and the Ars demonstrativa
stops.campa: Settled for a season at Montpellier, Ramon writes a longer and more rigorous version of his system, the Ars demonstrativa, and beside it something stranger: a novel, Blanquerna, following a man who rises from hermit to pope and then renounces even the papacy to return to solitude, the first romance of its kind in a vernacular tongue built to carry philosophy inside a story. Within its last book he sets a separate treatise, the Book of the Lover and the Beloved, mystical verses in the voice of a soul in love with God, as many, the book declares of itself, as the year has days.
stops.quote: The Lover asked his Beloved if there remained in Him anything still to be loved.
stops.quote_source: The Book of the Lover and the Beloved, verse 1 (within Blaquerna, Pt. V; trans. E. Allison Peers, 1923)

stops.name: Rome, the first audience, a dead pope
stops.campa: Ramon crosses to Rome to bring his whole design before the Holy See itself: the Art, the language schools, and beyond them a plan for the recovery of the Holy Land by preaching rather than only the sword. He arrives to find Pope Honorius IV dead and no successor yet seated, the curia scattered and unable to hear so large a petition from an unbeneficed layman of Majorca with no order and no title behind his name. He waits as long as he can afford, then turns north, carrying his papers and his patience to a university that will at least always sit still to argue.

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne, Felix and the doctors of the schools
stops.campa: At the end of the year Ramon reaches Paris and lodges near the schools of the Left Bank, frequenting the halls of the Sorbonne where he will be tolerated, argued with, and occasionally admired for the next twenty years of visits. Here he composes Felix, or the Book of Wonders, sending a wandering fool through the length of the created world, animal, vegetable, celestial, and human, to ask at every turn why things are as they are, wringing a small treatise on natural philosophy from a boy's naive questions. Doctors of the university, Peter of Limoges among them, begin to gather around his figures and wheels.

stops.name: Montpellier, the Art simplified, the friars' recommendation
stops.campa: Back at Montpellier through 1289 and into 1290, Ramon labors to cut his system down to a form students can actually hold in the memory, paring the great early Art toward what will become, after further revision, the Ars generalis ultima and its short companion the Ars brevis. The Franciscan order, whose habit and rule he has followed without formal vows since his conversion, commends his teaching to those who would learn it. He is close now to sixty, unbeneficed still, without a see or a chair, entirely dependent on the goodwill of princes and the patience of scholars for every road ahead.

stops.name: Genoa, the terror on the quay, the ship not boarded
stops.campa: In Genoa, waiting on a berth for Tunis, the mission he has planned and postponed for thirty years since the visions in his chamber, Ramon is seized by a terror he had not foreseen: that he will be caught on landing and rot the rest of his days in a Saracen prison, or die at once, unremembered and without the sermon he crossed the sea to preach. Feverish and shaking, he books passage on the first galley out and then, at the very quay, cannot make himself climb aboard; his friends, seeing him ill, hold him back from a ship he was in any case too broken to sail on.

stops.name: Genoa, the fever breaks, a new ship taken in secret
stops.campa: The fever and the terror pass, as fevers do, and within the year Ramon recovers his resolve along with his health. He books a second passage, and this time tells no one, not even the friends who kept him from the first ship, boarding before dawn so no hand of affection can hold him back again. He is past sixty, has never in his life crossed to Africa, and knows exactly, from the terror already lived through once, what he is sailing toward; he sails anyway, judging a coward's death by inches worse than whatever waits in Tunis.

stops.name: Tunis, the challenge to the doctors of the law
stops.campa: Ramon lands at Tunis in September and, once his Arabic has drawn a circle of the city's learned men around him, throws down a wager few missionaries before him have dared: let the doctors of Muslim law bring their strongest arguments, and if they can answer his reasons and convince him of the truth of Islam, he will become a Muslim on the spot. It is the whole logic of the Art turned outward into the street, argument alone, without a soldier behind it, staking his own soul on the wheels of the Dignities holding firm against the sharpest minds Tunis can set against them.

stops.name: Tunis, the public sermon, the death sentence commuted
stops.campa: Emboldened, or perhaps only faithful past the point of prudence, Ramon goes on to preach the Christian faith openly in the streets, a plain breach of the peace between the two kingdoms, which forbids preaching against Islam on Muslim ground. He is seized, beaten, and condemned by the emir to death by the sword. Only the intervention of the city's own mufti, together with resident Catalan and Genoese merchants who plead the value of peaceful trade over one troublesome friar's head, turns the sentence aside; he is expelled instead of beheaded, put aboard a ship under guard and told never to return.

stops.name: Naples, cast ashore, expelled
stops.campa: The guard-ship puts Ramon ashore at Naples in October, alive against the odds he had reckoned in Genoa the year before, his first African mission ended in expulsion rather than the martyrdom he had half expected and, by his own later admission, almost wished for. He does not go home to Majorca to recover but stays in the bustling Angevin port, taking up his pen again almost at once, already turning the failure at Tunis into material for the next version of his Art and the next appeal to whatever pope will next sit on the vacant throne of Rome.
